content: A person who attracts one mosquito species may be far less appealing to another. In a study involving 119 volunteers, researchers at Florida International University (FIU) found that three major disease-carrying mosquito species consistently preferred different people. Not a single participant was attractive to all three. The findings, published in iScience , challenge the idea that some people are universally irresistible to mosquitoes. Instead, attraction appears to depend on how individual species detect the chemicals and microorganisms associated with human skin. The researchers examined three species responsible for spreading diseases such as dengue, Zika, yellow fever, and West Nile virus. Each responded to a different combination of biological signals. Aedes aegypti , a mosquito that typically bites during the day, preferred people who wore no added fragrance and whose skin lacked certain volatile compounds. It also showed a slight preference for men. Another daytime feeder, Aedes albopictus (Asian tiger mosquito), was more attracted to people with elevated levels of ketones and plant-like chemicals naturally released by the skin. Culex quinquefasciatus (southern house mosquito), which feeds after dark, responded more strongly to differences in the skin microbiome. This community of bacteria, fungi, and other microorganisms varies from person to person. Certain bacterial families were associated with increased mosquito attraction, while others appeared to discourage feeding. Human scent contains more than 1,000 volatile organic compounds, many of which remain poorly understood. To investigate which biological characteristics influence mosquito attraction, the scientists collected odor and skin microbiome samples alongside their preference tests. Led by Ph.D. student Kaylee Marrero, the study was the first to directly compare how multiple mosquito species respond to the same individuals. The researchers had not anticipated such clear differences between species. “We didn’t expect the species to prefer different people when we started the study,” Marrero said. “Each species having a distinct microbial signature that they use as a cue was so surprising to me.” The results suggest that mosquitoes have evolved different ways of detecting and interpreting the complex chemical signals produced by human skin. “This connected so well with the differences in skin bacteria and odors,” said Matthew DeGennaro, a neurogeneticist who leads the research team and directs the Biomolecular Sciences Institute at FIU. “It is clear to me now that our skin microbiomes define our human odor signature. Each species found its own way to decode that signature.” Understanding which chemicals attract or discourage individual mosquito species could help researchers develop repellents designed to interfere with specific scent signals rather than relying on a universal approach. “Isolating the components of human odor that attract or repel mosquitoes could lead to novel strategies to combat vector-borne diseases,” DeGennaro said. By identifying the chemical compounds and microbial signatures associated with each species, the researchers are establishing a foundation for more targeted mosquito control. Future repellents could potentially be tailored to the species responsible for transmitting diseases in particular regions, although further research will be needed to translate these findings into effective protection. Reference: “Individual humans are more attractive to certain mosquito species” by Kaylee M. Marrero, John S. Castillo, Dani Lucas-Barbosa, Anthony J. Bellantuono, Matthew A. Marrero, Dariel Cid, Andre L. Costa-da-Silva, Niels O. Verhulst and Matthew DeGennaro, 31 July 2026, iScience . content: A new breakthrough in lithium separation could help overcome major challenges in extracting this essential battery material. A new technology developed at The University of Texas at Austin could make lithium extraction faster and more environmentally friendly by separating the valuable element from other dissolved substances with exceptional precision. The approach uses artificial channels so small they operate at the nanoscale, allowing lithium ions to pass through while blocking many competing ions. Inspired by the molecular gateways found in living cells, the channels demonstrated two to five times greater lithium selectivity than other recently developed lithium transporters. Researchers report that the structures rank among the most selective lithium channels created to date, offering a potential alternative to conventional extraction methods. Lithium is essential for batteries used in smartphones, electric vehicles, and electrical grids. It occurs in underground saltwater deposits known as brines, hard rock formations, and used batteries. However, these sources also contain elements such as sodium, potassium, magnesium, and calcium, whose ions can be difficult to separate from lithium. Existing extraction techniques often require considerable time and energy and can generate harmful waste. “Lithium is in our phones, our cars and the power grid, but getting it out of the ground cleanly is still a hard problem,” said Manish Kumar, a professor in the Fariborz Maseeh Department of Civil, Architectural and Environmental Engineering and the McKetta Department of Chemical Engineering who is one of the leaders of the new research published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society . “Our goal is a process that is faster, cleaner and easier to run.” The researchers designed tiny pores within membranes that mimic the selective transport pathways of biological cells. Their ability to distinguish lithium from other ions depends on two features working together: chemical groups positioned at the channel entrance and the tightly confined space inside. Interactions at the entrance, combined with the channel’s internal structure, favor lithium transport while restricting competing ions. The study builds on earlier research into separating rare earth elements , which are important for technologies including wind turbine magnets and electronic displays. By extending the underlying design principles to lithium, the researchers are developing a broader approach to selectively recovering critical minerals. “We now have a toolkit rather than a one-off result,” said Harekrushna Behera, a research scientist in Kumar’s lab. “By understanding how ions interact with the chemical groups at the channel entrance, we can work toward designing more selective channels for lithium and potentially other critical minerals.” The next challenge is incorporating these highly selective channels into membranes large enough for practical lithium recovery. The team is exploring a recently developed material made from interconnected, cell-like layers that can be constructed using lipids or plastic-like polymers. Such membranes could eventually support continuous lithium separation without harsh chemical solvents. Although the laboratory results demonstrate strong selectivity, the technology has not yet been validated for industrial extraction. Researchers still need to test its performance using real brines, where numerous dissolved salts coexist, and determine whether the channels can maintain their effectiveness at larger scales. Beyond recovering lithium from natural deposits, the researchers envision using the same technology to reclaim the element from discarded batteries. Another possible application is improving the separators inside batteries themselves, although further development will be needed to establish whether these uses are practical. Reference: “Highly Selective Artificial Lithium Channels” by Harekrushna Behera, Tyler J. Duncan, Laxmicharan Samineni, Hyeonji Oh, Chenhao Yao, Raman Dhiman, Siqi Wang, Luke Hatch, Venkat Ganesan and Manish Kumar, 24 October 2026, Journal of the American Chemical Society . DOI: 10.1021/jacs.6c13878 Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter. Follow us on Google and Google News .

content: Using advanced laser spectroscopy on extremely rare radioactive material, researchers have uncovered new insights into the structure of heavy atomic nuclei. The nucleus of fermium-255 is far from spherical. Scientists have now determined its shape for the first time, finding that it is strongly elongated, much like a rugby ball. The high-precision measurements, published in Physical Review Letters , also correct earlier nuclear data and provide new evidence supporting theoretical models of the heaviest elements. Fermium-255 contains 100 protons and 155 neutrons. In such heavy nuclei, the electrical repulsion between positively charged protons creates conditions that can lead to spontaneous fission, in which a nucleus splits into smaller fragments. Nuclear shape influences this process, making it a critical factor in predicting whether even heavier, potentially longer-lived elements can exist. Rather than observing the nucleus directly, researchers studied its interactions with the electrons surrounding it. Electrons close to the nucleus are sensitive to its size, shape, and magnetic properties. These interactions produce extremely small differences in atomic energy levels that can be detected through precise laser measurements. This phenomenon, known as hyperfine interaction, arises from the electromagnetic properties of the nucleus. A deformed nucleus interacts with the electric field of nearby electrons, while nuclear magnetism produces additional effects. Because fermium-255 has an odd number of neutrons, its nucleus also possesses a magnetic moment that contributes to the splitting of electronic energy levels. Scientists at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU) first observed atomic energy levels in fermium more than 20 years ago. However, the technology available then could not resolve the fine details needed to determine its nuclear structure accurately. Some of the resulting nuclear data remained incomplete or inconsistent. Fermium must be manufactured artificially, and obtaining enough atoms for an experiment requires an unusually complex production process. The researchers began with months of neutron irradiation of transuranium material at the High Flux Isotope Reactor at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (USA), producing einsteinium-254. After initial experiments in the United States, the material traveled to Mainz (Germany) for processing and then to the Institute Laue-Langevin in France for additional neutron irradiation. This produced einsteinium-255, which decays into fermium-255. The material was subsequently returned to Mainz for spectroscopy experiments. Einsteinium-255 has a half-life of approximately 40 days, allowing it to supply fermium-255 over several weeks. Through repeated chemical separations, scientists obtained individual samples containing tens of millions to about one billion fermium atoms. At JGU’s RISIKO separator, the samples were heated to approximately 1,000 degrees Celsius (1,832 degrees Fahrenheit) to release atoms for laser analysis. Specialized Ti laser systems excited and ionized the atoms, enabling researchers to resolve the hyperfine structure of two optical transitions despite the extremely small quantities available. Researchers combined the experimental spectra with advanced atomic calculations performed at Jagiellonian University in Kraków, Poland, and the Helmholtz Institute Mainz (HIM). The analysis confirmed that the fermium-255 nucleus has a strongly prolate shape, meaning it is stretched along one axis. It also produced a magnetic dipole moment that differs from previously tabulated values, correcting earlier results that were inconsistent with physical expectations. The measurements agree closely with modern nuclear theories developed by research groups in France and Germany. By providing more reliable information about nuclear deformation and magnetism, the findings strengthen models of nuclear fission and could improve predictions of the stability of superheavy elements that have yet to be discovered. Reference: “High-Resolution Laser Spectroscopy on the Hyperfine Structure of Fm255 (Z=100)” by Mitzi Urquiza-González, Matou Stemmler, Thomas E.
